1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: Modern Variations, Main Line

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Defends e4 and develops a piece. White gets a flexible set-up with an eye on queenside castling, and Black now chooses the pawn structure and the kind of game.
Defends e4 with a pawn instead of a piece, so the c-pawn stays free to take space later. The cost is a loosened kingside, and Black's reply in the centre gains time against the knight.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Prins Variation

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Apparently leaves e4 to its fate. If Black takes it, f7 comes under fire from the bishop and a queen coming to h5, and sacrifices on f7 expose the uncastled king. A tricky surprise, but not a move White can rely on.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Modern Variations, Ginsberg Gambit

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Hits the knight at once and takes central space. White's knight has to move, and Black's pawns on e5 and d6 leave d5 as a hole that Black must watch.
Takes b5 away from White's bishop and knights and prepares queenside expansion, while leaving the central set-up open. One of the most popular and most deeply studied systems against the open game.
Brings out the knight to its natural square and leaves the bishop's set-up for later. Black stays flexible, while White can choose between a sharp attack and calm development.

Prepares to fianchetto the bishop on the long diagonal, aiming at the queenside. In the sharpest lines White castles long and attacks the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside: an extremely sharp, complicated race.
A rare move that keeps the bishop ready to meet an exchange on b5 and can lead back to better-known set-ups. It avoids the main theory but spends a move on a bishop that no other main line needs.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Kupreichik Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Named after Viktor Kupreichik, its most frequent proponent.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Takes the centre at once, but the check on b5 follows and the exchange of light-squared bishops leaves the d5 square weak. White gets a knight outpost on f5 that Black can challenge only with concessions.
